reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Typically affects older adults, often with only trivial or forgotten head trauma weeks earlier, and is more common in those on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy
Presentation is usually insidious over days to weeks, with headache, confusion, gait disturbance, focal weakness, or a fluctuating conscious level that can mimic dementia or stroke
Brain atrophy in the elderly and in chronic alcohol use increases the subdural space and stretches bridging veins, predisposing to slow venous bleeding
On CT the collection is classically crescent-shaped over the convexity and hypodense or mixed density relative to acute blood; layering or membranes suggest recurrent bleeding of differing ages
Symptomatic collections causing mass effect are commonly managed with surgical drainage (burr-hole or craniotomy), while small asymptomatic collections may be observed
Correction of coagulopathy and careful review of anticoagulation are central to management and to reducing recurrence
Recurrence after drainage is relatively frequent, and subdural drains plus adequate brain re-expansion help lower this risk
Bilateral collections can mask midline shift, so symmetry on imaging should not be taken as reassurance
reference.pathophysiology: A chronic subdural haematoma is a slowly accumulating collection of blood and its breakdown products in the subdural space, between the dura and arachnoid. It often begins with minor tearing of bridging cortical veins, particularly where cerebral atrophy has enlarged the subdural space. An encapsulating membrane forms with fragile, leaky neovessels, and repeated micro-haemorrhages together with osmotic and inflammatory factors allow the collection to expand over weeks. Gradual enlargement produces mass effect on the underlying cortex, causing progressive or fluctuating neurological signs.
additionalDifferentials: Ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack
additionalInvestigations: Non-contrast CT head to identify the crescentic collection, its density, and midline shift
MRI brain when the diagnosis or age of blood is uncertain or isodense collections are suspected
Full blood count, coagulation profile, and platelet function assessment
Review of antiplatelet and anticoagulant medication and relevant drug levels or reversal targets
redFlags: Rapid deterioration in conscious level or new pupillary asymmetry suggesting acute rebleeding or herniation
Large collection with significant midline shift and effacement of basal cisterns
New or worsening focal deficit or seizures
Bilateral collections with clinical deterioration despite symmetric imaging
reference.prognosis: Many patients recover well after drainage of a symptomatic collection, but outcome is worse in the frail elderly and those with marked preoperative neurological impairment; recurrence and the need for repeat surgery are recognised problems.
pitfalls: Attributing gradual cognitive or gait decline to dementia and overlooking a treatable collection
Missing an isodense collection on CT, especially when bilateral and symmetric
Resuming anticoagulation without weighing rebleeding risk against thrombotic risk
Assuming complete resolution immediately after drainage when residual or recurrent collections are common
